sec05-card-sec05-F01.front: Where on the steering wheel—and with what thumb placement—should your hands sit for normal driving?
sec05-card-sec05-F01.expected_back: For normal driving, hold the outside rim of the steering wheel at the nine and three o'clock positions, with your thumbs resting along the face of the wheel.

sec05-card-sec05-F02.front: Why does holding nine and three matter specifically if the steering-wheel air bag deploys?
sec05-card-sec05-F02.expected_back: Holding the wheel at those positions lowers the risk of hand, wrist or arm injury if the air bag deploys.

sec05-card-sec05-F03.front: Which inward-facing steering grip must a driver never use while turning?
sec05-card-sec05-F03.expected_back: Never turn the steering wheel while holding it from the inside of the rim with your hand facing inward.

sec05-card-sec05-F04.front: For which two brief driving actions may one hand legally leave the steering wheel?
sec05-card-sec05-F04.expected_back: Both hands should stay on the wheel at all times except while shifting gears or giving hand signals.

sec05-card-sec05-R09.front: How firmly should you hold the wheel, and how does steering input change as speed rises?
sec05-card-sec05-R09.expected_back: Grip the wheel firmly but not too tightly, and hold it as steady as possible as speed increases.

sec05-card-sec05-F05.front: Where within your lane should you track, especially on a two-lane road with oncoming traffic?
sec05-card-sec05-F05.expected_back: Keep the vehicle centered in its lane, and on a two-lane road with oncoming traffic stay to the right.

sec05-card-sec05-F06.front: Up to how many degrees around the rim may your hands travel during hand-over-hand turning?
sec05-card-sec05-F06.expected_back: When steering hand-over-hand through a turn, the hands may travel as much as one hundred sixty-five degrees around the wheel.

sec05-card-sec05-R08.front: What turn range does hand-over-hand cover compared with what your hands do on a gentle curve?
sec05-card-sec05-R08.expected_back: Hand-over-hand steering covers adjustments from very small up to about half a turn of the wheel while both hands stay on it; in a gentle curve the hands usually keep their grip and make only slight finger or wrist movements.

sec05-card-sec05-R10.front: How do your pushing hand and crossing hand coordinate to start a hand-over-hand turn?
sec05-card-sec05-R10.expected_back: A hand-over-hand turn starts by pushing the wheel up from the nine or three o'clock position toward twelve while the other hand crosses over and down, after which the first hand returns to its starting position.

sec05-card-sec05-R11.front: Which two steering techniques straighten the front tires smoothly coming out of a turn?
sec05-card-sec05-R11.expected_back: To straighten after a turn, reverse the hand movements or let the wheel slide through the fingers (controlled slipping) while both hands stay on the wheel.

sec05-card-sec05-F07.front: In which four driving situations does hand-over-hand steering shine brightest?
sec05-card-sec05-F07.expected_back: Hand-over-hand steering works especially well for precision maneuvers, curves, entering and leaving intersections, and recovering from a skid.

sec05-card-sec05-F08.front: Which seven human, environmental, and mechanical variables govern total stopping distance?
sec05-card-sec05-F08.memory_hook: Driver, weather, weight, brakes, road, speed
sec05-card-sec05-F08.expected_back: Stopping distance depends on the driver's reaction time, weather and visibility, vehicle weight, brake condition, tire type and condition, the road surface and speed.

sec05-card-sec05-F09.front: Across every road and vehicle type, what single speed-and-stopping rule never changes?
sec05-card-sec05-F09.expected_back: One rule always holds: the faster a vehicle is moving, the longer it needs to stop.

sec05-card-sec05-R12.front: Is there a simple formula that predicts exact stopping footage for every car at a set speed?
sec05-card-sec05-R12.expected_back: There is no simple way to know exactly how long a vehicle will take to stop at a given speed.

sec05-card-sec05-F11.front: Under everyday traffic conditions, how long does a typical driver's reaction time take?
sec05-card-sec05-F11.expected_back: Under most traffic conditions, a typical driver's reaction time is three-quarters of a second.

sec05-card-sec05-F10.front: How many feet of pavement does your car cover every single second at sixty miles per hour?
sec05-card-sec05-F10.expected_back: At sixty miles per hour a vehicle covers eighty-eight feet every second.

sec05-card-sec05-R16.front: In New Jersey's stopping table, what reaction, braking, and total distances apply at ten miles per hour?
sec05-card-sec05-R16.expected_back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of nineteen feet at ten miles per hour, made up of eleven feet of reaction distance and eight feet of braking distance.

sec05-card-sec05-F12.front: What reaction distance, braking distance, and total stop does the manual list at twenty miles per hour?
sec05-card-sec05-F12.expected_back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of fifty-three feet at twenty miles per hour, made up of twenty-two feet of reaction distance and thirty-one feet of braking distance.

sec05-card-sec05-R13.front: What reaction, braking, and total stopping footage does the chart show at thirty miles per hour?
sec05-card-sec05-R13.expected_back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of one hundred two feet at thirty miles per hour, made up of thirty-three feet of reaction distance and sixty-nine feet of braking distance.

sec05-card-sec05-F13.front: At fifty miles per hour, how many reaction feet, braking feet, and total feet does stopping take?
sec05-card-sec05-F13.expected_back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of two hundred forty-seven feet at fifty miles per hour, made up of fifty-five feet of reaction distance and one hundred ninety-two feet of braking distance.

sec05-card-sec05-R14.front: At sixty miles per hour, what reaction, braking, and total stopping distances appear in New Jersey's chart?
sec05-card-sec05-R14.expected_back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of three hundred forty-three feet at sixty miles per hour, made up of sixty-six feet of reaction distance and two hundred seventy-seven feet of braking distance.

sec05-card-sec05-R15.front: What reaction, braking, and total stopping distances does the manual give at seventy miles per hour?
sec05-card-sec05-R15.expected_back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of four hundred fifty-three feet at seventy miles per hour, made up of seventy-seven feet of reaction distance and three hundred seventy-six feet of braking distance.

sec05-card-sec05-R17.front: Roughly how many feet per second does the manual state for typical braking deceleration?
sec05-card-sec05-R17.expected_back: The manual puts typical deceleration at approximately fourteen feet per second.

sec05-card-sec05-F14.front: What braking habit do beginners often get wrong, and what foot pressure produces controlled stops?
sec05-card-sec05-F14.expected_back: Slamming the brake pedal when there is no emergency is a common new-driver mistake that jerks the car to a stop and wears out brakes and tires; steady, gentle pressure gives a controlled stop.

sec05-card-sec05-F16.front: Which foot operates both the accelerator and brake, and what is the left foot's lone job in a stick-shift?
sec05-card-sec05-F16.expected_back: Use the right foot for both the brake and the gas pedal; with a manual transmission, the left foot works only the clutch.

sec05-card-sec05-R18.front: Does front-wheel versus rear-wheel drive change your braking technique—or what system actually matters?
sec05-card-sec05-R18.expected_back: Whether a vehicle has front-wheel or rear-wheel drive does not decide how to brake; what matters is knowing whether it has conventional drum and disc brakes or ABS.

sec05-card-sec05-F15.front: Even on dry asphalt at thirty-five miles per hour, what steering mistake can make an ABS car lose control?
sec05-card-sec05-F15.expected_back: A vehicle with anti-lock brakes may lose control at only thirty-five miles per hour, even on dry pavement, if the driver brakes while violently jerking the steering wheel.

sec05-card-sec05-R19.front: Where should new drivers get comfortable with how anti-lock pedal pulsing and steering feel?
sec05-card-sec05-R19.expected_back: Until they get used to ABS, new drivers are advised to rehearse hard stops and steering in an empty lot or another open space.

sec05-card-sec05-F17.front: Before which four everyday speed or path changes must you give a proper signal?
sec05-card-sec05-F17.expected_back: Give a proper signal whenever you turn, change lanes, stop or slow down.

sec05-card-sec05-F18.front: How far before a turn must your blinker click on in New Jersey, and what comes right after completing the turn?
sec05-card-sec05-F18.expected_back: Switch on the turn signal at least one hundred feet before turning, and cancel it after the turn so other drivers are not misled.

sec05-card-sec05-F19.front: How do you hold your left arm and palm to hand-signal stopping or slowing down?
sec05-card-sec05-F19.expected_back: The hand signal for stopping or slowing down is the arm extended downward with the palm facing the rear.

sec05-card-sec05-F20.front: Which direction does a driver extend the left arm to hand-signal a right turn?
sec05-card-sec05-F20.expected_back: The hand signal for a right turn is the arm extended upward.

sec05-card-sec05-F21.front: How does a driver hold the left arm out the window for a left turn?
sec05-card-sec05-F21.expected_back: The hand signal for a left turn is the arm held straight out.

sec05-card-sec05-R01.front: Can you line up downward, upward, and straight out with their three driver hand-signal meanings?
sec05-card-sec05-R01.memory_hook: Down stops, up right, out left
sec05-card-sec05-R01.expected_back: The three driver hand signals are easy to mix up: arm down with the palm to the rear means stop or slow, arm up means a right turn, and arm straight out means a left turn.

sec05-card-sec05-R02.front: What alternate right-turn hand signal may bicyclists, skateboarders, and inline skaters legally use?
sec05-card-sec05-R02.expected_back: Bicyclists, skateboarders and inline skaters use the same hand signals, but may also signal a right turn by holding the right arm straight out.

sec05-card-sec05-F22.front: Where is sounding your horn to alert a vehicle you are overtaking specifically appropriate?
sec05-card-sec05-F22.expected_back: A driver may sound the horn when passing another vehicle outside a business or residential zone.

sec05-card-sec05-F23.front: Under normal conditions, from at least how many feet away must a vehicle horn be heard?
sec05-card-sec05-F23.expected_back: Under normal conditions a horn must be audible from at least two hundred feet away.

sec05-card-sec05-F24.front: Which vehicles hold exclusive authority to mount sirens, whistles, or bells?
sec05-card-sec05-F24.expected_back: Sirens, whistles and bells are reserved for emergency vehicles.

sec05-card-sec05-R07.front: Why must you combine mirror checks with physically turning around before backing up?
sec05-card-sec05-R07.expected_back: Before backing up, make sure the path is clear by using the mirrors and also turning to look, because the view to the rear is limited.

sec05-card-sec05-F25.front: In reverse gear, which way does the rear of your car move when you turn the wheel right, left, or straight?
sec05-card-sec05-F25.expected_back: In reverse, turning the wheel to the right sends the vehicle to the right, turning it left sends it left, and holding it straight backs the vehicle straight.

sec05-card-sec05-R05.front: While turning the wheel in reverse, which way does the front nose of your vehicle swing?
sec05-card-sec05-R05.expected_back: While reversing, the front of the vehicle swings in the opposite direction from the turn.

sec05-card-sec05-F26.front: Where do your head, torso, right arm, and left hand go during straight-line backing?
sec05-card-sec05-F26.expected_back: To back up in a straight line, turn your head and body to the right so you can see out the back window without mirrors, rest your right arm over the front passenger seat, and hold the top of the wheel with your left hand.

sec05-card-sec05-F27.front: How fast—in miles per hour—should you normally roll while backing up?
sec05-card-sec05-F27.expected_back: Back up slowly, usually at walking speed of two to four miles per hour

sec05-card-sec05-F28.front: What must your wheels do before you shift out of Reverse into a forward gear?
sec05-card-sec05-F28.expected_back: Do not shift into a forward gear until the vehicle has come to a complete stop.

sec05-card-sec05-F29.front: Which one-handed reversing shortcut is dangerous and can fail you on the MVC road test?
sec05-card-sec05-F29.expected_back: Steering with one palm while turning in reverse is dangerous and can make an applicant fail the road test; use both hands while looking out the rear window.

sec05-card-sec05-F30.front: Roughly how far must an applicant back smoothly in a straight line during the New Jersey road test?
sec05-card-sec05-F30.expected_back: On the road test the applicant backs the vehicle about one hundred feet in a straight line, slowly and smoothly.

sec05-card-sec05-R04.front: Which two separate New Jersey rules—one on the road test and one on the street—use one hundred feet?
sec05-card-sec05-R04.expected_back: Two different figures of about one hundred feet are easy to confuse: the road test asks you to back up about one hundred feet in a straight line, and state law requires moving into the proper lane and signaling at least one hundred feet before any turn.

sec05-card-sec05-F31.front: Since August thirty-one, two thousand sixteen, how does the MVC treat factory backup cameras and sensors during road tests?
sec05-card-sec05-F31.expected_back: Since August thirty-one, two thousand sixteen, backup cameras and parking sensors installed on a vehicle may be used during the road test, but the basic reversing principles still come first.

sec05-card-sec05-F32.front: What is the only safe move if you overshoot a street corner or driveway turn?
sec05-card-sec05-F32.expected_back: If you miss a turn, never back up; taking the next turn is safer than risking a crash.

sec05-card-sec05-R06.front: Why must turns be planned well upstream, and how does faster traffic affect your timing?
sec05-card-sec05-R06.expected_back: Plan turns well ahead, since last-minute turns can be unsafe, and the faster traffic is moving the earlier the turn should be planned.

sec05-card-sec05-F33.front: Before starting any turn, where do you check your mirrors, and which smaller road users must you hunt for?
sec05-card-sec05-F33.expected_back: Before turning, check your mirrors behind and to both sides, and look for less visible road users such as motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds.

sec05-card-sec05-F34.front: When positioning for an upcoming turn, which comes first—moving into the turn lane or signaling?
sec05-card-sec05-F34.expected_back: Signal first, with the turn signal or a hand signal, and only then move into the proper lane for the turn.

sec05-card-sec05-R20.front: When do you shed speed for an intersection turn, and how should you drive through the arc itself?
sec05-card-sec05-R20.expected_back: Slow down before reaching the intersection, then keep a steady speed and follow the pavement markings through the turn.

sec05-card-sec05-F35.front: What lane discipline applies mid-turn, and what dashboard check follows straightening out?
sec05-card-sec05-F35.expected_back: Stay in the same lane until the turn is complete, then make sure the turn signal has switched off.

sec05-card-sec05-F36.front: Where on the roadway—and with what sightlines—should you begin a turnaround?
sec05-card-sec05-F36.expected_back: To turn around, start at the right edge of the road at a safe spot where you can see well in both directions.

sec05-card-sec05-F37.front: Walk through the three steering legs—and curb clearances—of a New Jersey K-turn?
sec05-card-sec05-F37.expected_back: In a K-turn, signal left and pull forward turning left to stop several inches from the left curb or street edge, back up turning right to stop several inches from the right curb or edge, then pull forward turning left and straighten the wheels.

sec05-card-sec05-F38.front: Which classic turnaround maneuver is mandatory for every new driver on the MVC road test?
sec05-card-sec05-F38.expected_back: A new driver is required to make the three-point turn, also called the K-turn, during the MVC road test.

sec05-card-sec05-F39.front: What two steps secure an automatic versus a manual vehicle every time you park?
sec05-card-sec05-F39.expected_back: Whenever you park, set the brake and put the vehicle in park, or for a manual transmission in reverse or low gear.

sec05-card-sec05-F40.front: When parking downhill beside a curb, which way do your front wheels point and what gear holds a stick-shift?
sec05-card-sec05-F40.expected_back: When parking downhill next to a curb, set the hand brake and turn the wheels toward the curb, with a manual transmission left in reverse.

sec05-card-sec05-F41.front: When parking uphill beside a curb, how do you angle the front wheels and set a manual gearbox?
sec05-card-sec05-F41.expected_back: When parking uphill next to a curb, set the hand brake and turn the wheels away from the curb, with a manual transmission left in low.

sec05-card-sec05-R03.front: How do wheel angle and manual gear choice flip between downhill curb parking and uphill curb parking?
sec05-card-sec05-R03.memory_hook: Down toward reverse, up away low
sec05-card-sec05-R03.expected_back: Downhill against a curb the wheels turn toward the curb and a manual gearbox goes in reverse, while uphill against a curb the wheels turn away from the curb and a manual gearbox goes in low.

sec05-card-sec05-R21.front: What checks, signals, and steering steps guide you cleanly into a right-hand angle parking space?
sec05-card-sec05-R21.expected_back: To enter an angle space on your right, watch traffic ahead and behind, signal and slow, make sure your rear end will clear the parked cars, steer sharply in, then straighten the wheels to center the vehicle and shift to park with the parking brake on.

sec05-card-sec05-R22.front: What physical check comes before climbing in to back out of an angle space, and how do you start reversing?
sec05-card-sec05-R22.expected_back: Before backing out of an angle space, walk around the vehicle to make sure nothing is in its way, then reverse slowly while making sure the lane is clear.

sec05-card-sec05-F42.front: How do you alert walkers and clear tall neighboring SUVs while backing out of an angle stall?
sec05-card-sec05-F42.expected_back: When backing out of an angle space, tap the horn to warn nearby pedestrians, and once you can see past the tops of the neighboring vehicles, stop and look again.

sec05-card-sec05-R23.front: At what exact clearance point do you straighten your wheels while backing out of an angle space?
sec05-card-sec05-R23.expected_back: When backing out of an angle space, keep turning slowly until the left front wheel passes the rear bumper of the car parked on the left, then straighten the wheels as you re-enter the traffic lane.

sec05-card-sec05-F43.front: How important is parallel parking on the MVC road test, and how much rehearsal does it demand?
sec05-card-sec05-F43.expected_back: An applicant must be able to parallel park to pass the MVC road test, and it is the maneuver that needs the most practice.

sec05-card-sec05-F44.front: How far apart should you space practice flags for parallel parking, and what does bumping one tell you?
sec05-card-sec05-F44.expected_back: To practice parallel parking, set out flags or markers twenty-five feet apart; hitting them means you are not ready to park between real vehicles.

sec05-card-sec05-F45.front: How many feet beside the forward parked car should you pull up to begin parallel parking?
sec05-card-sec05-F45.expected_back: To start parallel parking, pull up alongside the vehicle in front, about two to four feet away from it.

sec05-card-sec05-R24.front: Which two signals and visual check come right before backing into a parallel space?
sec05-card-sec05-R24.expected_back: Before backing into a parallel space, signal for a stop and signal right to show that you will back up to the right, then turn to check that the way behind is clear.

sec05-card-sec05-R25.front: Looking out the back window, how far do you roll straight back before cranking the wheel full right?
sec05-card-sec05-R25.expected_back: Looking out the rear window, back up slowly for about two feet and then turn the steering wheel fully to the right.

sec05-card-sec05-R26.front: What three things do you do once your front nose clears the rear bumper of the car ahead?
sec05-card-sec05-R26.expected_back: When the front of your vehicle clears the rear bumper of the car ahead, stop, check the angle and make sure the right rear wheel has not struck the curb.

sec05-card-sec05-R27.front: How do you steer, stop, and center to finish backing into a parallel space?
sec05-card-sec05-R27.expected_back: Next turn the wheel fully to the left while backing slowly, stop once the vehicle is in line without touching the car behind, then straighten the wheels and pull to the center of the space.

sec05-card-sec05-F46.front: At maximum, how many inches from the curb may a properly parallel-parked vehicle's tires sit?
sec05-card-sec05-F46.expected_back: A properly parallel-parked vehicle has its tires no more than six inches from the curb.

sec05-card-sec05-R28.front: What pace and pedal control make backing into tight parking stalls much easier?
sec05-card-sec05-R28.expected_back: The slower and smoother you back into a parking space, the easier parking becomes.

sec08-card-sec08-F01.front: What single factor causes the majority of motor vehicle crashes?
sec08-card-sec08-F01.expected_back: Most crashes are caused by driver error.

sec08-card-sec08-F02.front: What three steps make up the standard crash-prevention formula — and which three mindset habits back it up?
sec08-card-sec08-F02.expected_back: The standard crash-prevention formula is to be alert, be prepared and act in time: never assume other drivers will not make mistakes, expect the unexpected, and avoid panic.

sec08-card-sec08-R06.front: What should an angry or excited driver do before getting behind the wheel, and why?
sec08-card-sec08-R06.expected_back: Drivers who are angry or excited should take time to cool off before driving, because emotions strongly affect driving ability.

sec08-card-sec08-R07.front: Why isn't creeping noticeably slower than surrounding vehicles automatically the safest way to drive?
sec08-card-sec08-R07.expected_back: Some people assume driving slower than other vehicles is safer, but keeping up with the flow of traffic helps keep the road safe for everyone.

sec08-card-sec08-F03.front: How does the New Jersey manual define aggressive driving, and which five unlawful acts illustrate it?
sec08-card-sec08-F03.expected_back: Aggressive driving is a progression of unlawful acts such as sudden changes of speed, improper or erratic lane changes, ignoring traffic control devices, failing to yield and following too closely.

sec08-card-sec08-R08.front: What two duties still apply on a right turn on red, and how does the manual view rolling past without a complete stop?
sec08-card-sec08-R08.expected_back: A right turn on red still requires a full stop and yielding to traffic and pedestrians, and an incomplete stop counts among the dangers of ignoring traffic control devices.

sec08-card-sec08-R09.front: What triggers road rage, and what dangerous driving moves or hostile signals display it?
sec08-card-sec08-R09.expected_back: Road rage happens when drivers lose their temper over a traffic disturbance, and it shows up as running stop signs and red lights, speeding, tailgating, weaving, illegal passing on the right, gestures, screaming, honking or flashing high beams.

sec08-card-sec08-R10.front: What specialized law-enforcement resource does New Jersey deploy in its campaign against road rage?
sec08-card-sec08-R10.expected_back: New Jersey runs specially trained enforcement patrols as part of its campaign against road rage.

sec08-card-sec08-F05.front: Even when an emergency legally permits a handheld phone call, what is still the safest way to place it?
sec08-card-sec08-F05.expected_back: Even though the handheld phone law has emergency exceptions, the safest choice is to stop at the roadside first and only then place a call.

sec08-card-sec08-F06.front: Name and define the four categories of driving distraction?
sec08-card-sec08-F06.expected_back: The four types of driving distraction are visual (eyes off the road), manual (hands off the wheel), cognitive (mind off driving) and auditory (sounds that pull attention away).

sec08-card-sec08-F07.front: Where do distractions rank among teen crash causes, and how far does a car travel during a few distracted seconds at highway speed?
sec08-card-sec08-F07.expected_back: Distractions are one of the leading causes of crashes for teen drivers, and a few seconds of inattention at highway speed can cover the length of a football field.

sec08-card-sec08-F08.front: Beyond texting and scrolling, which everyday cabin habits — from GPS, music, and food to passengers and smartwatches — count as distractions?
sec08-card-sec08-F08.expected_back: Common distractions include texting, scrolling or watching videos, using a phone even hands-free, programming a GPS while moving, picking music, taking photos, eating or drinking, turning to talk to passengers, reaching for items and using smart watches.

sec08-card-sec08-F09.front: What three effects does fatigue have on a driver, and how dangerous can drowsy driving become?
sec08-card-sec08-F09.expected_back: A tired driver reacts more slowly, gets upset more easily, may fall asleep at the wheel, and can be as dangerous as a drunk driver.

sec08-card-sec08-F10.front: Enacted in June two thousand three, what does Maggie's Law make illegal and how does it classify sleepless fatal crashes?
sec08-card-sec08-F10.expected_back: Maggie's Law, enacted in June two thousand three, makes it illegal to knowingly drive while impaired by lack of sleep and treats fatigued driving as recklessness under the vehicular homicide statute.

sec08-card-sec08-F11.front: What is highway hypnosis, and what eye-movement habit prevents it?
sec08-card-sec08-F11.expected_back: Highway hypnosis is a trance-like state after long periods at the wheel, and it can be avoided by never fixing your eyes on one thing for more than a few seconds.

sec08-card-sec08-F12.front: How frequently should you stop to rest on a long trip — or what partner option keeps fatigue away?
sec08-card-sec08-F12.expected_back: On long drives, rest every two hours or share the driving with another licensed driver.

sec08-card-sec08-F13.front: Which drivers — by sleep debt, trip style, medication, age, or work schedule — face the highest drowsy-driving risk?
sec08-card-sec08-F13.expected_back: Those most at risk of drowsy driving include sleep-deprived people, drivers on long trips without breaks or driving when they would normally sleep, people on sleep-inducing medicine or alcohol, solo drivers, drivers on long rural roads, young people, shift workers and commercial drivers.

sec08-card-sec08-F14.front: Which four visual, audible, or headlight cues help you communicate your intentions or presence to other drivers?
sec08-card-sec08-F14.expected_back: Communicate with other drivers by turn or hand signals, eye contact, a tap of the horn when needed, and at night a quick switch from low beams to high and back.

sec08-card-sec08-R11.front: How should your lane choice telegraph an upcoming turn?
sec08-card-sec08-R11.expected_back: Always stay in the lane that shows the direction you intend to turn.

sec08-card-sec08-R12.front: What steering habits fit town or city traffic, and what lights belong on whenever you pull off the road?
sec08-card-sec08-R12.expected_back: Be patient in town or city traffic, avoid quick turns or lane changes, and switch on the emergency flashers whenever you must pull off the road.

sec08-card-sec08-F23.front: What lane-straddling mistake must you avoid, and what three-step check-and-signal sequence makes a lane change safe?
sec08-card-sec08-F23.expected_back: When changing lanes, never straddle a lane: check the rearview mirror, glance back at the blind spot and always signal.

sec08-card-sec08-R17.front: Which three necessity, speed, and marking conditions must all hold true before you pass or change lanes?
sec08-card-sec08-R17.expected_back: Pass or change lanes only when necessary, only if it can be done without speeding, and only where signs and pavement markings allow it.

sec08-card-sec08-F24.front: After overtaking a car, what mirror cue confirms you are far enough ahead to signal right, return, and cancel your blinker?
sec08-card-sec08-F24.expected_back: After passing, signal and return to the right lane only when well ahead of the passed vehicle, a good sign being that you can see it in your rearview mirror, then cancel the signal.

sec08-card-sec08-F25.front: What lane and speed response helps an overtaking driver pass you safely, and when do you resume normal speed?
sec08-card-sec08-F25.expected_back: When another vehicle passes you, stay in your lane and slow down to make the pass easier, then resume normal speed once it is well ahead.

sec08-card-sec08-F15.front: What is tailgating, and what multi-car crash pattern does it commonly trigger?
sec08-card-sec08-F15.expected_back: Tailgating means following the vehicle ahead too closely; it is a common cause of crashes and can set off a chain of rear-end collisions.

sec08-card-sec08-R13.front: How should you position inside your lane and manage space around all sides of your vehicle?
sec08-card-sec08-R13.expected_back: Keep space on all sides of the vehicle, stay in the middle of the lane, and make sure there is room ahead to stop or pass safely.

sec08-card-sec08-F16.front: How many car lengths — and roughly how many feet — does the traditional rule of thumb add per ten miles per hour, and when do you add more?
sec08-card-sec08-F16.expected_back: The usual rule of thumb is to stay one car length, about twenty feet, back for every ten miles per hour of speed, and to leave more room at high speed or in bad weather.

sec08-card-sec08-R05.front: While one twenty-foot car length per ten miles per hour is common, does the New Jersey manual consider any following rule perfect?
sec08-card-sec08-R05.expected_back: The car-length rule of thumb is one length, roughly twenty feet, for every ten miles per hour, although the manual admits no following-distance rule is perfect.

sec08-card-sec08-F17.front: Walk through how you use a fixed roadside object to apply New Jersey's three-seconds-plus following rule?
sec08-card-sec08-F17.expected_back: Under the three-seconds-plus rule, pick a fixed object ahead, start counting when the vehicle in front passes it, and you have enough room for a sudden stop if you need at least three seconds to reach it.

sec08-card-sec08-F18.front: To how many seconds should you stretch your following interval in bad weather?
sec08-card-sec08-F18.expected_back: In bad weather, lengthen the following interval to four seconds or more.

sec08-card-sec08-R01.front: Compare your minimum time cushion under the three-seconds-plus rule on normal dry pavement versus bad weather?
sec08-card-sec08-R01.expected_back: The three-seconds-plus rule calls for at least three seconds behind the vehicle ahead in normal conditions, and the interval rises to four or more seconds in bad weather.

sec08-card-sec08-R14.front: What road conditions do standard time and distance following guidelines assume, and what payoff comes from practicing them?
sec08-card-sec08-R14.expected_back: The time and distance guidelines assume the best driving conditions, and practicing good following distance helps you stop safely and smoothly if the vehicle ahead stops.

sec08-card-sec08-F19.front: Which three distances add together to make total stopping distance?
sec08-card-sec08-F19.expected_back: The manual defines stopping distance as perception distance plus reaction distance plus braking distance.

sec08-card-sec08-F20.front: What foot habit trims reaction distance, and how does vehicle weight affect total stopping distance?
sec08-card-sec08-F20.expected_back: Keeping a foot close to the brake reduces reaction distance, and heavier vehicles may take longer to stop.

sec08-card-sec08-R15.front: What maintenance awareness should you keep on your brakes, and how should following distance shift on wet, snowy, or icy roads?
sec08-card-sec08-R15.expected_back: Know the condition of your brakes, test them often and allow more following distance whenever road conditions are poor, especially on wet, snowy or icy roads.

sec08-card-sec08-F21.front: On ideal pavement, how many minimum car lengths does the manual's table list at twenty, thirty, forty, and fifty miles per hour?
sec08-card-sec08-F21.expected_back: The manual's minimum following distance table for ideal roads is two car lengths at twenty miles per hour, three at thirty miles per hour, four at forty miles per hour and five at fifty miles per hour

sec08-card-sec08-F22.front: How do the minimum car lengths in the manual's table change on wet pavement across twenty, thirty, forty, and fifty miles per hour?
sec08-card-sec08-F22.memory_hook: Doubles to four, six, eight, ten
sec08-card-sec08-F22.expected_back: On wet pavement the table doubles those figures to four car lengths at twenty miles per hour, six at thirty miles per hour, eight at forty miles per hour and ten at fifty miles per hour

sec08-card-sec08-R16.front: In New Jersey's minimum following distance table, how do the car lengths for gravel compare with wet pavement?
sec08-card-sec08-R16.expected_back: In the manual's minimum following distance table, gravel calls for the same car lengths as wet pavement: four at twenty miles per hour, six at thirty miles per hour, eight at forty miles per hour and ten at fifty miles per hour

sec08-card-sec08-F26.front: How must your speed, braking, and steering inputs change on wet roads, and why?
sec08-card-sec08-F26.expected_back: On wet roads, drive more slowly, stop and turn with great care, and avoid quick turns or speed changes that can start a skid.

sec08-card-sec08-F27.front: At roughly what speed can tires start hydroplaning on a film of water, and what happens as speed climbs?
sec08-card-sec08-F27.expected_back: Tires can begin to hydroplane, riding on a film of water, at about thirty-five miles per hour, and the risk grows as speed increases.

sec08-card-sec08-F28.front: What happens to tire contact, braking, and steering on wet roads above fifty-five miles per hour?
sec08-card-sec08-F28.expected_back: Above fifty-five miles per hour tires may lose contact with the road entirely, and then braking becomes virtually impossible and turning impossible.

sec08-card-sec08-R02.front: Separate New Jersey's two hydroplaning speed benchmarks — where it can begin versus where tires can lose road contact entirely?
sec08-card-sec08-R02.expected_back: Hydroplaning can begin at about thirty-five miles per hour, but above fifty-five miles per hour the tires may leave the road surface altogether.

sec08-card-sec08-F29.front: What tire rule, speed habit, and lane-position trick help prevent hydroplaning during heavy rain?
sec08-card-sec08-F29.expected_back: To avoid hydroplaning, do not drive on bald or badly worn tires, slow down in heavy rain, standing water or slush, and in a downpour use the highest part of the road, such as the center lane.

sec08-card-sec08-R18.front: Once a vehicle is hydroplaning on water, which three minor forces are enough to spin it into a skid?
sec08-card-sec08-R18.expected_back: While a vehicle is hydroplaning, even a wind gust, a shift in the level of the road or a gentle turn can start a skid.

sec08-card-sec08-F30.front: How should you warm up your engine and clear your vehicle's exterior before driving in cold winter weather?
sec08-card-sec08-F30.expected_back: In cold weather, warm up the engine as the manufacturer directs and remove all snow and ice from the entire vehicle before driving.

sec08-card-sec08-F31.front: Who is legally responsible in New Jersey if ice flies off a moving vehicle and causes death, injury, or property damage?
sec08-card-sec08-F31.expected_back: New Jersey law holds a driver responsible for ice that flies off the vehicle and causes death, injury or property damage.

sec08-card-sec08-R19.front: What visibility and weather hazards multiply in winter, and what reservoir fluid must be winter-ready?
sec08-card-sec08-R19.expected_back: Winter brings extra dangers such as longer darkness, fog, rain, snow, sleet and ice, and the vehicle should carry the proper type of windshield washer fluid.

sec08-card-sec08-R21.front: After how many consecutive minutes is vehicle idling prohibited in New Jersey, and which situations are exempt?
sec08-card-sec08-R21.expected_back: Idling for more than three consecutive minutes is prohibited, with exceptions that include vehicles stopped in traffic, being repaired or waiting for inspection, emergency vehicles in emergencies, and buses loading or unloading passengers.

sec08-card-sec08-R24.front: Before pulling out in frost or ice, how must you prepare your vehicle's glass and climate system?
sec08-card-sec08-R24.expected_back: Before starting in frost or ice, scrape and wipe every window and turn on the defroster.

sec08-card-sec08-F32.front: Which three driver mistakes break tire traction and start a skid?
sec08-card-sec08-F32.expected_back: A vehicle skids when the driver accelerates too quickly, turns too fast or brakes improperly.

sec08-card-sec08-R20.front: How can you safely test just how slick a snowy or icy road is — and what else does that test reveal?
sec08-card-sec08-R20.expected_back: To judge how slippery a snowy or icy road is, brake gently while driving slowly, which also shows how fast you can go and still stop safely.

sec08-card-sec08-F33.front: On snow and ice, how does proper pedal technique differ between ABS brakes and conventional disc or drum brakes?
sec08-card-sec08-F33.expected_back: On snow and ice, drivers with ABS keep a foot on the brake pedal without pumping, while conventional disc and drum brakes need firm, steady pressure.

sec08-card-sec08-F34.front: If conventional non-ABS brakes lock up on slick pavement, how should you work the brake pedal until control returns?
sec08-card-sec08-F34.expected_back: If conventional brakes lock, release the pedal and reapply at once with slightly less pressure, repeating with less and less pressure until the vehicle is under control.

sec08-card-sec08-R03.front: Contrast what your foot does on snow and ice with ABS versus locked conventional brakes?
sec08-card-sec08-R03.expected_back: With ABS on snow and ice, keep a foot on the brake and never pump, but with conventional brakes that lock, release and reapply with gradually less pressure.

sec08-card-sec08-F35.front: Where do winter snow tires fall short, and what equipment delivers the best grip on ice and deep or hard-packed snow?
sec08-card-sec08-F35.expected_back: Snow tires give better traction in winter but not on ice, and tire chains give the best traction on ice and in hard-packed or deep snow.

sec08-card-sec08-R04.front: What three maneuvers do snow tires assist in snow — and why do tire chains still win in severe winter conditions?
sec08-card-sec08-R04.expected_back: Snow tires help with starting, steering and stopping in snow but do not grip well on ice, whereas tire chains give the best traction on ice and in hard-packed or deep snow.

sec08-card-sec08-F36.front: Between which exact calendar dates are studded snow tires legal on New Jersey roads?
sec08-card-sec08-F36.expected_back: In New Jersey, studded snow tires may be used between November fifteen and April one.

sec08-card-sec08-F37.front: What throttle, gear, and rocking techniques help get a vehicle moving on snow or ice?
sec08-card-sec08-F37.expected_back: To start on snow or ice, keep the engine speed low, shift to a lower gear if the wheels spin, and rock between forward and reverse if stuck.

sec08-card-sec08-F38.front: How many seconds of following distance does the manual recommend on snow-covered roads?
sec08-card-sec08-F38.expected_back: On snow-covered roads, a good rule is a following distance of six seconds or more.

sec08-card-sec08-F39.front: What speed and two lighting choices belong whenever you drive through fog?
sec08-card-sec08-F39.expected_back: In fog, always slow down, keep the headlights on low beam and switch on fog lights if the vehicle has them.

sec08-card-sec08-F40.front: When fog, snow, or heavy rain cuts visibility severely, where should you go and what lights do you switch on?
sec08-card-sec08-F40.expected_back: Whenever visibility is greatly reduced, pull off alongside the road or onto the shoulder, out of traffic, and turn on the emergency flashers.

sec08-card-sec08-R22.front: If your windshield defroster quits during freezing rain or snow, what three steps help warm the glass?
sec08-card-sec08-R22.expected_back: If the defroster stops working in freezing rain or snow, stop safely, close the windows and let the heater warm them.

sec08-card-sec08-R23.front: Which four visor, steering, speed, and visual habits counter blinding sun glare?
sec08-card-sec08-R23.expected_back: Against sun glare, set the visors to shade your eyes without blocking the road, hold the wheel firmly, slow down and watch the lane markings.

sec15-card-sec15-F01.front: Whose command must you obey when a police officer directing traffic gives an instruction that conflicts with the traffic light?
sec15-card-sec15-F01.expected_back: A police officer directing traffic can overrule the traffic signals, and a driver must always obey law enforcement orders and directions.

sec15-card-sec15-F02.front: What legal consequence awaits anyone caught stealing or vandalizing traffic, airport, or railroad-crossing signs or equipment?
sec15-card-sec15-F02.expected_back: Stealing or damaging airport, traffic or railroad-crossing signs or equipment brings court penalties.

sec15-card-sec15-F03.front: From top to bottom on a vertical traffic light—and on the left of a horizontal light—how are signal colors arranged?
sec15-card-sec15-F03.expected_back: On a vertical signal, red is always on top, yellow in the middle and green third, with any green arrow at the bottom; on a horizontal signal, red is always on the left.

sec15-card-sec15-F04.front: Where must you bring your vehicle to a halt at a steady red light, and when may you proceed?
sec15-card-sec15-F04.expected_back: At a red light, stop before the intersection or crosswalk and stay stopped until the light turns green.

sec15-card-sec15-F05.front: What does a steady yellow traffic light require unless you are already too close to brake safely?
sec15-card-sec15-F05.expected_back: At a steady yellow light, stop before entering the intersection or crosswalk unless you are too close to stop safely.

sec15-card-sec15-F06.front: What signal transition does a yellow arrow warn you is about to happen?
sec15-card-sec15-F06.expected_back: A yellow arrow warns that the light is about to go from green to red, giving you time to stop safely.

sec15-card-sec15-F07.front: Whom must you still yield to on a green light—including before making a left turn?
sec15-card-sec15-F07.expected_back: On a green light, go ahead but yield to pedestrians and vehicles still in the intersection, and before turning left yield to oncoming vehicles.

sec15-card-sec15-F08.front: How may you move when facing a green arrow—even alongside a red bulb—and whom must you still yield to?
sec15-card-sec15-F08.expected_back: A green arrow, alone or together with a red light, lets you go only in the direction the arrow points, while still yielding to pedestrians.

sec15-card-sec15-R06.front: How does pressing a pedestrian push button affect signal timing at an intersection?
sec15-card-sec15-R06.expected_back: At signals with pedestrian push buttons, pressing the button soon changes the flow so the side street gets a longer green.

sec15-card-sec15-F09.front: How should you respond when approaching a flashing yellow signal?
sec15-card-sec15-F09.expected_back: A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with care.

sec15-card-sec15-F10.front: What three steps does a flashing red traffic light require?
sec15-card-sec15-F10.expected_back: A flashing red light means stop, yield to traffic and pedestrians, and go only when it is safe.

sec15-card-sec15-R01.front: What is the core operational difference between a flashing yellow signal and a flashing red signal?
sec15-card-sec15-R01.expected_back: A flashing yellow light only asks you to slow down and take care, but a flashing red light requires a full stop before going on when safe.

sec15-card-sec15-F12.front: How must every driver treat an unlit traffic signal when power is out and no officer is directing traffic?
sec15-card-sec15-F12.expected_back: A signal with no working bulbs and no one directing traffic must be treated as a four-way stop.

sec15-card-sec15-F13.front: What does a steady orange raised-palm pedestrian signal mean for people at the curb versus people mid-crosswalk?
sec15-card-sec15-F13.expected_back: When pedestrians face a steady orange raised palm, they must not step off the curb, and anyone already in the crosswalk will have time to finish crossing.

sec15-card-sec15-F14.front: What does a white walking symbol or countdown allow pedestrians to do, and what does New Jersey law require of turning drivers?
sec15-card-sec15-F14.expected_back: On a steady white walking figure or countdown, pedestrians may cross, and New Jersey law requires turning drivers to yield to them.

sec15-card-sec15-F15.front: Into which three broad categories do road signs fall, and what job does each category perform?
sec15-card-sec15-F15.expected_back: Signs fall into three categories: warning signs for hazards that are hard to see, guidance signs that identify routes and destinations, and regulatory signs that control speed and movement.

sec15-card-sec15-F16.front: Which single traffic message owns the eight-sided red octagon?
sec15-card-sec15-F16.expected_back: A red octagon, with eight sides, is used only for STOP signs.

sec15-card-sec15-F17.front: Which traffic control sign uses the three-sided red triangle?
sec15-card-sec15-F17.expected_back: A red triangle, with three sides, is used for YIELD signs.

sec15-card-sec15-F18.front: What roadway restriction does a three-sided yellow pennant sign warn you about?
sec15-card-sec15-F18.expected_back: A yellow pennant, a three-sided shape, marks a no-passing zone warning.

sec15-card-sec15-F19.front: What type of zone or crossing does a five-sided yellow pentagon announce?
sec15-card-sec15-F19.expected_back: A yellow pentagon, with five sides, marks a school sign.

sec15-card-sec15-F21.front: What roadside activity does an orange diamond sign warn drivers to expect?
sec15-card-sec15-F21.expected_back: An orange diamond warns of construction and maintenance work.

sec15-card-sec15-F22.front: What distinct information do blue, brown, and green rectangular highway signs each provide?
sec15-card-sec15-F22.memory_hook: Blue services, brown parks, green routes
sec15-card-sec15-F22.expected_back: Blue rectangular signs give motorist services and information, brown ones point to public recreation and scenic areas, and green ones give direction guidance.

sec15-card-sec15-F24.front: What shape, background color, and legend color identify general roadway warning signs?
sec15-card-sec15-F24.expected_back: General warning signs are yellow diamonds with a black symbol or word message.

sec15-card-sec15-R08.front: Beyond general cautions, which two specific warning categories also use the yellow diamond?
sec15-card-sec15-R08.expected_back: A yellow diamond is also used for roadway hazard and railroad crossing warning signs.

sec15-card-sec15-F23.front: When do highway engineers mount a smaller advisory speed plaque together with a curve or turn warning?
sec15-card-sec15-F23.expected_back: When the safe speed on a curve or turn is lower than the posted limit, an advisory speed sign is posted with the warning sign.

sec15-card-sec15-R07.front: Which two background colors may pedestrian and bicycle warning signs use, and what action do they demand?
sec15-card-sec15-R07.expected_back: Pedestrian crossing and bicycle warning signs may be standard yellow or an optional yellow-green, and they tell drivers to share the road with and yield to pedestrians and cyclists.

sec15-card-sec15-F25.front: Which five conditions do orange road-work diamonds warn about—and how do New Jersey traffic fines change there?
sec15-card-sec15-F25.expected_back: Orange diamond road work signs warn of lane closings, lane shifts, flaggers, uneven pavement and detours, and in New Jersey all traffic fines double in work zones.

sec15-card-sec15-R10.front: What enforceable sign type is commonly posted right alongside orange work-zone warnings?
sec15-card-sec15-R10.expected_back: Reduced speed limit signs are posted alongside orange work zone signs.

sec15-card-sec15-R09.front: Which four spacing, reading, braking, and scanning habits keep everyone safe inside a road-work zone?
sec15-card-sec15-R09.expected_back: Near road work, control your following distance and reaction time, read and follow the signs, be ready to slow or stop, and watch for workers and moving machinery.

sec15-card-sec15-F26.front: How much legal authority does a construction-zone flagger hold—and what happens if you ignore one?
sec15-card-sec15-F26.expected_back: A flagger has the same authority as a regulatory sign, so a driver who disobeys one can be cited.

sec15-card-sec15-R16.front: What does a fluorescent, reflective orange triangle mounted on the back of farm or construction gear signify?
sec15-card-sec15-R16.expected_back: A fluorescent, reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle marks a slow-moving vehicle, such as farm or construction equipment on a public highway.

sec15-card-sec15-F27.front: What shape and color scheme do most regulatory traffic signs use?
sec15-card-sec15-F27.expected_back: Regulatory signs are usually vertical rectangles with black wording and border on a white background.

sec15-card-sec15-F28.front: How are the shape, background, lettering, and borders arranged on a standard YIELD sign?
sec15-card-sec15-F28.expected_back: A YIELD sign is a white inverted triangle with red wording and a red border inside a white border band.

sec15-card-sec15-F30.front: Describe the shape, colors, central bar, and text layout of a DO NOT ENTER sign?
sec15-card-sec15-F30.expected_back: A DO NOT ENTER sign is a white square holding a red circle crossed by a horizontal white band, with the words in white above and below the band.

sec15-card-sec15-F31.front: How do green national truck route signs differ in meaning from red national truck signs?
sec15-card-sec15-F31.expected_back: Green national truck signs mark routes and ramps where trucks are allowed, while red ones mark where trucks are prohibited or where designated routes end.

sec15-card-sec15-F20.front: How do the round yellow railroad sign and the white X-shaped sign divide advance warning versus track location?
sec15-card-sec15-F20.expected_back: A white X marks a railroad crossing, and a round yellow sign is the advance warning that a railroad crossing is ahead.

sec15-card-sec15-F29.front: Which regulatory sign does a white railroad crossbuck match in legal meaning—and why must cars always yield?
sec15-card-sec15-F29.expected_back: The crossbuck, a white X-shaped railroad sign with black lettering, means the same as a Yield sign, and drivers must always yield to trains because trains cannot swerve.

sec15-card-sec15-F11.front: What do flashing red railroad lights announce, and when is it legal to drive across the tracks?
sec15-card-sec15-F11.expected_back: Flashing red lights at a railroad crossing mean a train is coming, and you may go only after they stop flashing and every other active warning device shuts off.

sec15-card-sec15-R02.front: Which three railroad crossing markers count as passive warnings, and which three count as active warnings?
sec15-card-sec15-R02.expected_back: Pavement markings, signs and crossbucks are passive railroad warning devices, while flashing red lights, ringing bells and lowered gates are active warnings.

sec15-card-sec15-F32.front: How does the legal authority of painted road markings compare with posted signs and overhead signals?
sec15-card-sec15-F32.expected_back: Road markings carry the same force of law as signs and traffic signals.

sec15-card-sec15-F33.front: How do yellow roadway lines and white roadway lines tell you which direction neighboring traffic moves?
sec15-card-sec15-F33.expected_back: Yellow center lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, while white lines separate lanes moving the same way and mark road edges.

sec15-card-sec15-F34.front: What do a broken centerline stripe versus a solid centerline stripe on your side allow regarding passing?
sec15-card-sec15-F34.expected_back: A dashed line on your side of the center line means you may pass when it is safe, and a solid line on your side means you may not pass.

sec15-card-sec15-R04.front: When a solid yellow stripe runs beside a dashed yellow stripe, who may pass and by what point must the pass finish?
sec15-card-sec15-R04.expected_back: With a solid yellow line and a dashed yellow line side by side, pass only when the dashed line is on your side, and finish the pass before the dashes turn solid.

sec15-card-sec15-R05.front: What passing and lane-discipline rules apply along double solid yellow or double solid white lines?
sec15-card-sec15-R05.expected_back: Double solid yellow and white lines prohibit passing, so never cross a solid yellow line to pass, stay in your lane and keep right when driving slowly.

sec15-card-sec15-R11.front: What do painted lane arrows paired with signs require, and what do white dashed highway lines separate?
sec15-card-sec15-R11.expected_back: Road arrows used with other signs show the direction a driver must take from that lane, and white dashed lines separate lanes on multi-lane highways.

sec15-card-sec15-R12.front: What boundary do white and yellow highway edge lines mark for drivers?
sec15-card-sec15-R12.expected_back: Edge lines separate the shoulder from the travel lane and mark the edge of the highway, and yellow edge lines do the same job.

sec15-card-sec15-R13.front: Where must you stop when a white stop line is painted versus when no stop line is painted?
sec15-card-sec15-R13.expected_back: Where no stop line is painted, stop before the crosswalk when a sign, signal or pedestrian requires you to stop, and where a white stop line exists, stop at it.

sec15-card-sec15-R14.front: What purpose do oversized white pavement words like STOP AHEAD, SCHOOL, and RXR serve?
sec15-card-sec15-R14.expected_back: White special pavement markings such as STOP AHEAD, SCHOOL and RXR alert drivers to special conditions ahead.

sec15-card-sec15-R15.front: What do painted or signed white diamonds reserve a lane for, and where do you find the active rules?
sec15-card-sec15-R15.expected_back: White diamonds on signs or painted in the lane mark high occupancy vehicle (HOV) lanes reserved for certain vehicles or for vehicles carrying several riders, and posted signs give the operating hours.

sec15-card-sec15-R03.front: How does a street speed bump differ physically from a speed hump?
sec15-card-sec15-R03.expected_back: A speed bump is a low ridge across the street, while a speed hump is a longer, flatter version.

sec15-card-sec15-R17.front: How do rumble strips alert drivers, do they harm your tires or suspension, and what usually accompanies them?
sec15-card-sec15-R17.expected_back: Rumble strips vibrate the wheel and make noise to warn of a decision point ahead or wake a dozing driver; they do not damage the vehicle and usually come with a caution sign.

sec15-card-sec15-R18.front: How does traffic circulate inside a roundabout, and why do roundabouts slash severe intersection crashes?
sec15-card-sec15-R18.expected_back: A roundabout is a one-way circular intersection around a center island, and because traffic enters and exits only by right turns, severe crashes are greatly reduced.

sec10-card-sec10-F01.front: How does alcohol distort a driver's thinking—even in small amounts when someone feels below the limit?
sec10-card-sec10-F01.expected_back: Alcohol can make a driver overconfident and unable to think clearly, and even a small amount raises the chance of a crash, including when the driver believes they are under the legal limit.

sec10-card-sec10-F02.front: Which five physical or visual driving skills start slipping after two, three, or four drinks?
sec10-card-sec10-F02.expected_back: After two, three or four drinks, alcohol starts to impair reaction time, coordination and balance, and it also dulls vision and the ability to judge distance.

sec10-card-sec10-R08.front: Which emotional state paired with alcohol drives much of the reckless aggression behind fatal highway crashes?
sec10-card-sec10-R08.expected_back: Alcohol paired with anger accounts for much of the reckless, aggressive driving behind fatal highway crashes.

sec10-card-sec10-F04.front: How many vehicles are involved in most alcohol-related crashes, and who still ends up killed or hurt?
sec10-card-sec10-F04.expected_back: Most alcohol-related crashes involve a single vehicle, yet they often kill or seriously injure several people, including passengers, pedestrians and other drivers.

sec10-card-sec10-F03.front: What is the sole cure for intoxication, and in what percentages does your body clear alcohol?
sec10-card-sec10-F03.expected_back: Only time sobers a person up: the liver burns off about ninety percent of the alcohol and the other ten percent leaves through breath, urine and sweat, which is why quick sober-up tricks fail.

sec10-card-sec10-F13.front: How much pure alcohol sits inside five ounces of wine, twelve ounces of beer, or a one-and-a-half-ounce whiskey shot?
sec10-card-sec10-F13.expected_back: One and a half ounces of eighty-proof whiskey, twelve ounces of beer and five ounces of wine each hold about the same half ounce of alcohol.

sec10-card-sec10-F14.front: In studies cited by the New Jersey manual, what beverage had most arrested drunk drivers been drinking?
sec10-card-sec10-F14.expected_back: According to the studies the manual cites, beer is what most drivers arrested for drunk driving had been drinking.

sec10-card-sec10-F05.front: What is the sole scientific measure of alcohol in your system, and what quick test checks it?
sec10-card-sec10-F05.expected_back: Blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, is the only scientific measure of how much is too much, and a simple breath test reveals it.

sec10-card-sec10-F06.front: Which four personal or drinking variables determine your Blood Alcohol Concentration?
sec10-card-sec10-F06.expected_back: BAC depends on four factors: how much alcohol was consumed, body weight, how quickly the drinks went down, and what food was eaten.

sec10-card-sec10-F15.front: How does eating affect alcohol absorption, and can food stop a high BAC or sober you up?
sec10-card-sec10-F15.expected_back: Food slows how fast alcohol enters the blood, but it cannot prevent a high BAC during steady heavy drinking and it does not make anyone sober.

sec10-card-sec10-R03.front: Why won't eating a big dinner protect a heavy drinker from hitting a high BAC?
sec10-card-sec10-R03.expected_back: Eating slows alcohol absorption, but heavy drinking always produces a high BAC whatever was eaten.

sec10-card-sec10-F07.front: Which drug categories and adult BAC threshold make driving illegal in New Jersey?
sec10-card-sec10-F07.expected_back: New Jersey makes it illegal to drive while impaired by liquor or by narcotic, hallucinogenic or habit-forming drugs, and also to drive with a BAC at or above zero point zero eight percent.

sec10-card-sec10-F08.front: At what tiny BAC does a driver younger than twenty-one break New Jersey law?
sec10-card-sec10-F08.expected_back: For a driver younger than twenty-one, driving with a BAC of zero point zero one percent or higher is illegal and carries severe penalties on top of any DUI penalties.

sec10-card-sec10-R01.front: How does New Jersey's adult per-se BAC limit contrast with the under-twenty-one threshold?
sec10-card-sec10-R01.expected_back: The adult limit is a BAC of zero point zero eight percent, while a driver under twenty-one breaks the law at just zero point zero one percent.

sec10-card-sec10-F09.front: Just past which BAC mark does your statistical risk of causing a crash double?
sec10-card-sec10-F09.expected_back: At a BAC slightly above zero point zero five percent, the risk of causing a crash doubles.

sec10-card-sec10-F10.front: By what multiples does crash risk jump at point one zero BAC and point one five BAC?
sec10-card-sec10-F10.expected_back: Crash risk is six times as great at a BAC of zero point one zero percent and twenty-five times as great at zero point one five percent.

sec10-card-sec10-R02.front: How do crash-risk multipliers escalate across New Jersey's three cited BAC benchmarks?
sec10-card-sec10-R02.expected_back: Crash risk roughly doubles just above zero point zero five percent BAC, climbs to six times at zero point one zero percent and to twenty-five times at zero point one five percent.

sec10-card-sec10-F11.front: What four core penalties hit a driver who refuses a breath test in New Jersey?
sec10-card-sec10-F11.expected_back: Refusing a breath test is illegal in New Jersey, and penalties include losing driving privileges, referral to an Intoxicated Driver Resource Center (IDRC), fines and an ignition interlock device.

sec10-card-sec10-F12.front: What extra financial assessment follows a breath-test refusal, and what happens if you leave it unpaid?
sec10-card-sec10-F12.expected_back: A driver who refuses a breath test also owes a violation surcharge, and leaving it unpaid suspends driving privileges indefinitely until it is paid.

sec10-card-sec10-F16.front: Which five driving behaviors are New Jersey officers trained to spot as telltale drinking clues?
sec10-card-sec10-F16.expected_back: Police are trained to watch for five telltale signs of a drinking driver: speeding, weaving, unusually slow driving, jerky changes of speed and abrupt stops at signs or lights.

sec10-card-sec10-R04.front: Why do officers treat unusually slow driving—not just speeding—as an impairment red flag?
sec10-card-sec10-R04.expected_back: Slow driving can also signal impairment, because an intoxicated driver may be overly cautious and fall below the normal flow of traffic.

sec10-card-sec10-R05.front: Must a car cross painted lane lines for police to spot impaired weaving?
sec10-card-sec10-R05.expected_back: Weaving can show up even when an intoxicated driver stays inside the correct lane, because holding a straight line becomes hard.

sec10-card-sec10-R06.front: What causes an impaired driver's jerky speed changes and abrupt stops at intersections?
sec10-card-sec10-R06.expected_back: Jerky driving means short mental lapses that keep an intoxicated driver from holding a steady speed on a clear road, and quick stops mean braking suddenly at a sign or light instead of easing up.

sec10-card-sec10-R07.front: What is the one guaranteed way to prevent a drinking-and-driving crash, and which three ride options fit?
sec10-card-sec10-R07.expected_back: The surest way to avoid a drinking-and-driving crash is not to drive at all after drinking, and the manual suggests a designated driver, public transportation or a cab instead.

sec10-card-sec10-R09.front: Whom does a designated driver protect by getting drinking friends or family home sober?
sec10-card-sec10-R09.expected_back: A designated driver takes responsibility for getting friends or family who have been drinking home safely, which also protects other motorists.

sec10-card-sec10-F19.front: Which designated-driver campaign did New Jersey become the first state in the nation to launch officially?
sec10-card-sec10-F19.expected_back: New Jersey was the first state to officially launch the Hero Campaign for designated drivers.

sec10-card-sec10-F17.front: What three drink-and-food habits define a responsible party host?
sec10-card-sec10-F17.expected_back: A good host offers alcohol-free drinks and nourishing food, never pushes drinks or refills, and stops serving alcohol well before the party ends.

sec10-card-sec10-F18.front: How should a host handle an impaired guest, when are police called, and what legal risk hits the host?
sec10-card-sec10-F18.expected_back: If a guest has had too much, do not let them drive: suggest a nap or an overnight stay, call the police only as a last resort, and remember that a host can be sued over a guest's drunk-driving crash.

sec10-card-sec10-F20.front: What two drug-related conditions make driving illegal on New Jersey roads?
sec10-card-sec10-F20.expected_back: It is illegal to drive in New Jersey while under the influence of any drug, or while carrying any drug without a valid prescription.

sec10-card-sec10-F22.front: What must you show police when driving with prescription medication, and what if you lack proof?
sec10-card-sec10-F22.expected_back: Drivers using prescription drugs must show proof of the prescription to police when asked, and a drug that requires a prescription is treated as illegal if the driver has none.

sec10-card-sec10-F21.front: How should you respond to a drowsiness or dizziness label, and which common medicines impair driving?
sec10-card-sec10-F21.expected_back: Do not take a medicine labeled as possibly causing drowsiness or dizziness before driving; cold pills, tranquilizers and some prescription drugs can affect basic driving skills.

sec10-card-sec10-R10.front: Whom must you consult before combining medications, and what substance must never mix with any drug?
sec10-card-sec10-R10.expected_back: Never combine drugs without asking a medical professional about side effects and driving, and never mix alcohol with any drug or medication.

sec10-card-sec10-R11.front: Why should you ask a pharmacist or doctor before driving on an over-the-counter medication?
sec10-card-sec10-R11.expected_back: Ask a professional how an over-the-counter drug may affect driving, because legal medicines can still impair.

sec10-card-sec10-F23.front: Right behind alcohol, which substance turns up most frequently in crash-involved drivers?
sec10-card-sec10-F23.expected_back: After alcohol, marijuana is the drug most often found in drivers involved in crashes.

sec10-card-sec10-F24.front: Which four lane, gap, alertness, and attention skills can marijuana weaken behind the wheel?
sec10-card-sec10-F24.expected_back: Marijuana can weaken a driver's tracking (staying in the lane), distance judgment, vigilance and ability to divide attention among many tasks.

sec10-card-sec10-R12.front: Can everyday aches like a stiff neck, cough, or sore leg hurt safe driving—and what should you do?
sec10-card-sec10-R12.expected_back: Any health problem, even a stiff neck, a cough or a sore leg, can interfere with driving, so let someone else drive when you feel unwell.

sec10-card-sec10-F25.front: How often does the manual recommend vision checks generally—and once you pass age forty?
sec10-card-sec10-F25.expected_back: Have your eyes tested every year or two, and every year once you are over age forty.

sec10-card-sec10-R16.front: What re-screening power does New Jersey state law grant the MVC over licensed drivers?
sec10-card-sec10-R16.expected_back: State law allows the MVC to retest the driving population.

sec10-card-sec10-R13.front: How does healthy side—or peripheral—vision help while you look straight down the road?
sec10-card-sec10-R13.expected_back: Good side (peripheral) vision lets a driver notice things out of the corners of the eyes while still looking straight ahead.

sec10-card-sec10-R14.front: Why does distance judgment matter constantly around traffic and parked obstacles?
sec10-card-sec10-R14.expected_back: Poor distance judgment is a frequent cause of crashes, so a driver should always know how far the vehicle is from nearby objects.

sec10-card-sec10-R15.front: Why does sharp hearing matter in traffic, and what two audio habits keep your ears open?
sec10-card-sec10-R15.expected_back: Hearing matters because horns, sirens and screeching tires give warnings, so keep the radio low and never drive wearing earphones.

sec13-card-sec13-F01.front: While pedestrian safety is shared, who holds the primary duty to prevent crashes with people on foot—and why?
sec13-card-sec13-F01.expected_back: Pedestrian safety is shared, but drivers carry the primary duty to prevent crashes with pedestrians, who are the most vulnerable road users.

sec13-card-sec13-F02.front: How does a struck pedestrian's fatality risk jump between twenty miles per hour and forty miles per hour?
sec13-card-sec13-F02.expected_back: A pedestrian struck by a car at twenty miles per hour has about a five percent chance of dying, but at forty miles per hour that rate jumps to eighty-five percent.

sec13-card-sec13-F03.front: Does an intersection corner without painted white lines still have a legal crosswalk, and what is it called?
sec13-card-sec13-F03.expected_back: Every corner of an intersection has a crosswalk even when no lines are painted, and this is called an unmarked crosswalk.

sec13-card-sec13-F04.front: How does New Jersey distinguish a driver's legal duty at a marked crosswalk versus an unmarked crosswalk?
sec13-card-sec13-F04.expected_back: Drivers must stop and stay stopped for a pedestrian in a marked crosswalk, and yield to a pedestrian crossing in an unmarked one.

sec13-card-sec13-F05.front: What must you do if the pedestrian signal switches to don't walk mid-crossing, and what two crosswalk actions are barred?
sec13-card-sec13-F05.expected_back: If the signal changes from WALK to DON'T WALK while a pedestrian is crossing, the driver must still stop, and a driver may never block or park in a crosswalk or pass a vehicle stopped at one.

sec13-card-sec13-F06.front: Which five consequences can follow failing to stop for a pedestrian—and what escalates the penalty further?
sec13-card-sec13-F06.expected_back: Failing to stop for a pedestrian can mean fines, possible jail, community service, points and license suspension, with tougher penalties if serious bodily injury results.

sec13-card-sec13-F07.front: Where should you stop before a crosswalk on a multi-lane road when a pedestrian is crossing—and why?
sec13-card-sec13-F07.expected_back: On a road with several lanes, stop well short of the crosswalk so you do not hide the pedestrian from drivers in the next lanes.

sec13-card-sec13-F08.front: What rules bind pedestrians at crossings, and does a walker's mistake ever excuse a careless driver?
sec13-card-sec13-F08.expected_back: Pedestrians must obey signals and may not step suddenly into the path of a car too close to yield, but their mistakes never excuse a driver from using due care.

sec13-card-sec13-F09.front: Around which five community zones—and which curbside hazard—should you slow down and watch for children?
sec13-card-sec13-F09.expected_back: Slow down in school zones and near bus stops, playgrounds, parks and business districts, and watch around parked vehicles where pedestrians, especially children, may appear.

sec13-card-sec13-F10.front: What full visual check is required before any turn—especially before turning right on red?
sec13-card-sec13-F10.expected_back: Before any turn, and especially a right on red, scan left, right and behind, check mirrors and blind spots, and look for pedestrians in or entering the crosswalk.

sec13-card-sec13-R06.front: Why do so many pedestrian collisions happen during turns, and which three off-street access points demand extra vigilance?
sec13-card-sec13-R06.expected_back: Many pedestrian crashes happen during turns because drivers watch only for other vehicles, so watch for pedestrians when entering or leaving driveways, parking lots and alleys.

sec13-card-sec13-R07.front: How should drivers adjust speed and attention for pedestrians after dark or during poor weather?
sec13-card-sec13-R07.expected_back: Pedestrians are harder to see at night and in poor weather, so drivers must slow down and stay more alert after dark.

sec13-card-sec13-R08.front: How should pedestrians walk and dress at night where sidewalks are absent—and how does that affect your duty?
sec13-card-sec13-R08.expected_back: Pedestrians walking where there are no sidewalks should face traffic and wear reflective or light-colored clothing at night, but that never relieves drivers of their duty to stay vigilant.

sec13-card-sec13-F12.front: Do standard traffic laws apply to motorcycles, and how should you check blind spots before turning or changing lanes?
sec13-card-sec13-F12.expected_back: Laws for cars and trucks also apply to motorcycles, but a rider may react differently, so check blind spots twice before changing lanes or turning.

sec13-card-sec13-F13.front: Why must you never tailgate a motorcycle in traffic?
sec13-card-sec13-F13.expected_back: Never follow a motorcycle too closely, because it may be able to stop in a shorter distance than other vehicles.

sec13-card-sec13-F14.front: How should you manage your speed and lane position while a motorcycle is passing your vehicle?
sec13-card-sec13-F14.expected_back: When a motorcycle passes you, keep your speed and position and give it room to finish the pass.

sec13-card-sec13-F15.front: What single driver failure causes the majority of motorcycle collisions?
sec13-card-sec13-F15.expected_back: The most common cause of motorcycle crashes is a driver failing to notice and recognize the motorcycle in traffic.

sec13-card-sec13-R09.front: Which road-surface textures threaten motorcycle stability and can trigger a sudden lane swerve?
sec13-card-sec13-R09.expected_back: Slippery, sloped or uneven pavement and grooves or gratings are hazards for motorcycle riders, so anticipate a rider swerving around something a car would ignore.

sec13-card-sec13-R10.front: Where do motorcycles demand extra visual scanning, and what signaling and spacing habits protect riders?
sec13-card-sec13-R10.expected_back: Watch for motorcycles at intersections and when turning left, always signal, and leave plenty of room between your car and a motorcycle.

sec13-card-sec13-R11.front: Before turning, parallel parking, opening a car door, or pulling from a curb, how must you check blind spots?
sec13-card-sec13-R11.expected_back: Before turning, parallel parking, opening a door or pulling from the curb, check blind spots by turning your head rather than relying on mirrors alone.

sec13-card-sec13-F16.front: By how much can bad weather stretch the stopping distance of a truck, tractor-trailer, or bus?
sec13-card-sec13-F16.expected_back: In bad weather a truck, tractor-trailer or bus may need as much as twenty-five percent longer to stop.

sec13-card-sec13-F17.front: What does New Jersey call the areas around a truck or bus where its driver cannot see you in the mirrors?
sec13-card-sec13-F17.expected_back: When a truck or bus driver cannot see your vehicle in their rearview or side mirrors, your vehicle is sitting in a no-zone, or blind spot.

sec13-card-sec13-F18.front: How should you position yourself when a truck is backing up or preparing to back—and why?
sec13-card-sec13-F18.expected_back: Stay well back from a truck that is getting ready to back up or is backing, and never pass close behind it, because the area behind it is a blind spot for everyone.

sec13-card-sec13-F19.front: How far behind a large truck or bus should you travel, and what multi-truck position should you avoid?
sec13-card-sec13-F19.expected_back: Hang farther back than usual behind a large truck or bus so that you show up in its driver's mirrors, and never get sandwiched between large vehicles.

sec13-card-sec13-F20.front: Why must you stop with extra buffer behind a large truck or bus at a traffic light, especially facing uphill?
sec13-card-sec13-F20.expected_back: When stopped behind a large vehicle at a light or sign, leave room, especially facing uphill, because it may roll back slightly as it starts.

sec13-card-sec13-F21.front: How may a long truck set up a right turn, and how should nearby drivers respond?
sec13-card-sec13-F21.expected_back: A truck may need to swing wide to the left to make a right turn, so give it extra road space.

sec13-card-sec13-F22.front: When may you merge back in front after passing a truck, and which passing side is strictly off-limits?
sec13-card-sec13-F22.expected_back: After passing a truck, do not pull back in front until you can see its entire front in your rearview mirror, and never pass a truck on the right.

sec13-card-sec13-F23.front: What should you avoid alongside a truck's trailer, and how should you steer when a large vehicle approaches oncoming?
sec13-card-sec13-F23.expected_back: Do not linger in the long blind spots along a truck's sides, and bear right when a large vehicle comes toward you to reduce wind turbulence and the risk of a sideswipe.

sec13-card-sec13-F24.front: Who must yield when a bus re-enters traffic from a passenger stop, and what penalties hit violators?
sec13-card-sec13-F24.expected_back: All non-emergency vehicles must yield to a bus re-entering traffic after picking up or dropping off passengers, and violators face a fifty dollars to two hundred dollars fine, up to fifteen days in jail, or both.

sec13-card-sec13-R02.front: Once a bus has rejoined normal moving traffic, does New Jersey's special bus-yield law cover its lane changes?
sec13-card-sec13-R02.expected_back: The bus yield rule covers a bus re-entering traffic from a stop, but once the bus is back in the normal flow, drivers do not have to yield when it changes lanes.

sec13-card-sec13-F26.front: What legal rights, duties, and New Jersey classification apply to bicyclists, skateboarders, and inline skaters?
sec13-card-sec13-F26.expected_back: Bicyclists, skateboarders and inline skaters have the same rights and duties as motor vehicles, and New Jersey classes them as vulnerable road users.

sec13-card-sec13-F11.front: What three progressive options does New Jersey's Safe Passing Law require when overtaking a covered road user?
sec13-card-sec13-F11.expected_back: Under the Safe Passing Law, move over one lane when you can, leave at least four feet when passing on a single-lane road, and if four feet is impossible slow to twenty-five miles per hour and be ready to stop.

sec13-card-sec13-R03.front: Under the Safe Passing Law, does giving space and slowing down let you break speed limits or no-passing zones?
sec13-card-sec13-R03.expected_back: Due caution under the Safe Passing Law means slowing down and giving plenty of space, while still obeying every no passing and speed law and moving over a lane when one is available.

sec13-card-sec13-F27.front: How do the fine and license points compare for breaking the Safe Passing Law without injury versus causing bodily injury?
